title: Pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)
hookLine: always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things
carry: a thread that runs through the whole day

cards: Paul had barely started a church in Thessalonica, a port city in northern Greece, when trouble broke out and the believers sent him away by night. He tried to go back and couldn't.

So he wrote to a young church he was worried about. Today begins a new stretch, from Thessalonians to Philemon. And near the end of this first letter, Paul packs a whole way of life into three short commands.

teach.h: HOW COULD ANYONE PRAY WITHOUT CEASING?
teach.b: "Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In all things give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you all." Three words in the middle. Pray without ceasing.
How could anyone do that? You have to sleep, cook, answer emails. Christians have given several answers.
Saint Augustine said the desire of the heart is itself a prayer: if your longing for God never stops, your prayer never stops, even while your lips are busy with something else.
Eastern Christians developed the Jesus Prayer, a short line repeated with the breath until it runs underneath everything.
An old Russian book, The Way of a Pilgrim, tells of a man who hears this very verse read in church and sets out walking to learn how to do it.
The Catholic Church's answer includes the Liturgy of the Hours: psalms and prayers at set times, morning, evening and night, so that, as the Church sees it, the whole day is offered to God.
The Angelus bell, rung in some places morning, noon and evening, does the same thing for anyone within earshot. Now look at the third command.

teach.h: IN ALL THINGS, NOT FOR ALL THINGS.
teach.b: In all things give thanks. In, not for. Paul isn't asking anyone to be grateful for cancer or for prison.
He's saying there's something to give thanks for even inside a hard thing. He'd know. He was run out of Thessalonica, and he still opens this letter saying he gives thanks for them always.
Pray without ceasing, then, isn't nonstop talking. It's a thread that runs through the whole day.

how: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours at set times of day, and some pray the Angelus, traditionally at six, noon and six; Catholics also use short repeated prayers, sometimes called aspirations, throughout the day.

o: a vow of silence kept for a whole season
without interval: prayer running through the day
nonstop words, praying aloud every minute

games.q: three short commands — tap the pairs.
p: the heart's desire is a prayer

s: 'give thanks in all things' means be grateful for suffering
in, not for: something to give thanks for inside a hard thing.
Paul left Thessalonica in a hurry
the believers sent him away by night, and he could not get back.
praying without ceasing means talking to God nonstop
Christians understand it as desire, short prayers, and prayer at set hours woven through the day.

games.q: you've just heard 'pray without ceasing' read aloud. what does the pilgrim in the old Russian story do?
o: decide it's impossible and forget it.
set out walking to learn how.
pray only on Sundays to make up for it.
games.why: in The Way of a Pilgrim he sets out to find someone who can teach him, and learns the Jesus Prayer.

practice: Choose a short line to carry: if you pray, the Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner, or Paul's three words; if not, a plain word, like thanks.
Say it silently as you breathe in, and again as you breathe out. When your mind wanders, come back without scolding yourself, and let it run underneath, the way the pilgrim learned to.
